Darr didn’t hear the creak of the floorboard till he was already rolling off the bed, his boots scraping the dust on the floor like a horse slipping on gravel. The bedframe groaned, split in two where the old nail had given way, and the splintered wood caught his boot and sent a sharp jolt up his leg. He spat into the dirt, didn’t even blink. “You said you’d keep the gate open,” he grumbled, pointing at the rusted post by the stable door. “Now the wind’s got the whole west side of the yard in a choke.”

Bronc stood there, hands still on the splintered edge of the bed, one finger pressed to his jaw like he’d just remembered he had a toothache. “I did,” he said, voice dry as a sunbaked boot heel. “But that don’t mean the wind don’t get to ride in. You can’t tell a man to stay still when the wind’s got a mind of its own.” He turned, slow, and looked at Darr with that same old half-smile—like he’d seen this before, maybe in a dream. “And if the gate’s open, maybe it’s not the wind that’s got the whole damn place in a choke. Maybe it’s the men who don’t know how to close it.”

The rig coughed, spitting black smoke that curled like a dying dog’s breath, and the oil lamp on the dash flared out, casting long shadows across the cracked dashboard. "Well, I reckon we ain't got no more gas," Jules said, wiping sweat from his brow with the back of his hand, "but I can still smell the horse in the dirt where the trail splits." He looked at Mitch, eyes narrowed, like he was trying to read a map written in dust. "You said you were gonna bring the old Pinto, but it's not even in the corral. Must’ve been a good ten miles off the road, that one." Mitch just stared at the cracked leather seat, where a single boot had left a smear of mud, and the silence stretched like a rope pulled too tight. Then, out of nowhere, the engine sputtered again, and the rig lurched forward—just enough to make the seatbelt snap back with a sharp *crack*.

He shoved his hat back on, wiped a hand across his brow, and said, “Well, I’ll need a saddle with no stirrups—just the leather, raw and hot from the sun.” He pulled a rusted iron ring from his boot and held it up. “This one’s from the old McAllister ranch, near the red rock pass. Used to hold a rope to a dead mule. Still sharp enough to cut a man’s boot off if he didn’t pay his rent.”  

“You’re going to ride a bull, aren’t you?” she said, squinting at the ring. “A real one—no fence, no crowd, just you and it in the dust.” He nodded. “Not a show bull. A mountain-born, one that’s never seen a corral. I’ll take the old buck from the west fork, the one that knocked over a wagon in ’37. I’ll ride it like a man rides a storm—no warning, no mercy.” She leaned back, hands tucked in her coat. “Then you’ll show me the fur, won’t you? The real, living fur?” He grunted. “Like it’s breathing.”

He leaned in, breath hot against her cheek, and she flinched, eyes wide, before he pressed his lips to her temple—just a brush, like a feather on stone. The wind snatched the last of the smoke from the stove, and the cabin groaned as if in protest.  

"Damn near forgot I had a rifle in the saddle," he said, pulling it from the scabbard with a grunt. "Felt it shift when you moved."  

She didn’t answer, just stared at the rusted lock of the door, where a piece of broken wood stuck out like a tooth. A bullet had once hit it, she remembered—no one’d seen it happen. Now it was just a dent, and the smell of old oil and wet leather hung in the air like a promise.  

He set the rifle on the table, fingers brushing the trigger guard. "You want to go back to the bunkhouse? Or do you wanna stay and see if that old woman down the lane still has her porch light on?"  

She looked at him, slow, like she was trying to read the shape of something she’d missed before.

Josh shifted, his boots scraping the dirt, and Darrin felt the weight of him shift from the horse to his chest, the boy’s body pressing into the old leather of his coat like it was trying to find a place to rest. The horse exhaled a long, slow breath and lowered its head, its eyes half-lidded, as if it had been watching the whole thing, waiting for the moment when the two men would stop talking and just *be*.  

“Horse’s been quiet since the feed run,” Darrin muttered, his voice rough, like gravel dragged over iron. “Didn’t bark when the coyotes came. Didn’t even stir when the wind blew the dust into the corral.” He glanced at Josh, who was staring at the line of fence where the sun had just vanished behind the old windbreak. “Like it knew you were coming.”  

Josh didn’t answer right away. Just stood there, hands still on Darrin’s shoulders, and when he spoke, it was low, almost a whisper: “I was just a kid when I first saw you ride in on that busted wagon, back in ’78. You were all dust and sweat and that smell of burnt oil. I thought you’d never say anything about the way you looked at the sky when you stopped to rest.”  

And then he smiled—slow, tired, like he’d been holding it in for years—and Darrin realized he wasn’t just waiting for this. He was remembering it, too.

The saloon door slapped shut behind them, the sound like a gunshot in the quiet. The cowboy wiped his palms on his jeans and stepped toward the bar, where the light from the oil lamp flickered over a stack of dirty poker chips and a half-empty bottle of whiskey labeled "Sour Sides." He didn’t need to look—knowing the place like the back of his hand, he pulled the bottle from the shelf, poured a stiff shot into a chipped mug, and tossed it back like a man who’d already lost the fight.  

The woman at the end of the table shifted, her boots tapping a slow rhythm on the floorboards. "You said you didn’t want to go back to the old ways," she said, not looking up. "But you’ve been eyeing that ledger for two days straight."  

"Old ways?" The cowboy grinned, a sharp, tired thing. "I just wanted to know if the land had a soul before I sold it." He set the mug down. "Now that I know it's just a paper trail, I'm gonna keep it warm. And if it gets cold, I’ll burn it in the stove."

The lantern on the mantel flickered, casting long shadows across the floorboards. Jake didn’t look up from the saddle he was retying, the leather splitting under his fingers like old bones. “Yeah, I do,” he said, not unkindly. “But you don’t get to just walk out the door and leave it all behind. You got to stay in the saddle till the wind turns, even if you’re tired.”  

He leaned back, one boot scraping against the wood, and gave the horse a sharp tap with his heel. “I’ve seen men try to ride off like they won’t come back, only to find the whole damn town’s gone by the time they get to the next bend. This place don’t just take you in — it eats you up slow, like a rusted hinge.”  

The wind picked up outside, rattling the tin roof. Jake didn’t care. He just watched Josh’s hands move over the saddle, slow and careful, like he was learning how to hold something again — a rifle, a horse, or maybe just the weight of being alive.

Jesse cracked his whip on the porch post, the leather snapping like a dry bone. "You two talkin' about it like it's a rodeo run or a dry creek bed—like it’s just the wind and the sun that made it happen. But you don’t see the dust on the boots, do you? That’s the sign. That’s the real thing." He wiped sweat from his brow with the back of his hand, eyes flicking to the old windmill, its rusted blades spinning slow as a man who’d lost his mind.  

"Guess I didn’t know how to say it out loud," Darrin said, pulling his shirt down to the waist, the fabric loose at the seams. "Didn’t know if it was just me, or if it was the whole damn town—how we all kept turnin’ the same way in the dark, like we were all just waitin’ for the same damn thing to happen."  

Gregory stepped back, his boots scuffing the dirt, and looked down at his hands. "Then maybe it ain’t about what happens between us," he said, voice low. "Maybe it’s about what happens after. When you don’t look back, and you just keep walkin’—and the wind still knows your name."

Trent dropped the rusted key into the dust of the dry creek bed and kicked a rock hard enough to make the gravel pop. The sun was still high, the kind that bleeds through the dry sage and paints the sky a sickly yellow. He didn’t look back until he heard the mule cough, deep and wet, like a man trying to breathe through a broken pipe. 

“Damn it, old girl,” he muttered, half to himself, half to the wind. “You don’t get to die in a place like this, not after I paid you for the first six months of trail.” He pulled the leather satchel from his belt and shoved it into the saddlebag. The one with the brass locket inside—his mother’s, not his father’s—hadn’t been touched since he came back from the war. 

He turned the mule toward the red-rock ridge, the one that rose like a jagged tooth from the plain. The wind carried a smell of old oil and something sour, like the inside of a rusted barrel. The mule shifted its weight, and for a second, Trent thought he saw a shadow move behind the rocks—just tall enough to be a man, too thin to be a ghost. But when he looked again, the ridge was just the ridge. And the sun was still hot.

The boy didn’t flinch, just stiffened for a second like a horse caught in a fence, then let out a slow exhale. "Yeah, slow’s fine," he said, voice rough as sandpaper. "But don’t pretend it’s nothing. That ain’t how it rolls, not with a man like you." He shifted his weight, bracing his feet against the rusted gatepost, one hand still cupped in Josh’s grip.  

Josh grinned, a real one, the kind that cracked at the corners of his mouth like a dry creekbed. "I never said it was nothing," he replied, pressing his elbow into the boy’s side, making him wince. "Just that it ain’t got to be a bond, not right off the bat. You don’t need to say you’re married to it. You just gotta feel it—like the wind through the brush, like the dust when you ride too hard and the earth kicks back."  

The boy turned his head slightly, caught the corner of a shadowed barn where a rusted windmill creaked, its blades still spinning in the wind like a dying breath. "Then what’s the deal with the blue eyes?" he asked, eyes narrowing. "Was that a sign?"  

Josh laughed, low and sharp, and didn’t answer right away. Just leaned in a little more, his breath brushing the boy’s neck. "Maybe," he said. "Maybe it’s just a trick of the light, or the way the sun hits the range when the wind turns." Then he added, almost to himself, "Or maybe it’s the only thing that ever looked like it knew me before I did."

Josh’s hand slid down the boy’s shoulder, brushing the edge of his worn leather jacket, and he didn’t stop until it found the brass buckle at his belt. "You ain’t got nothin’ on but that shirt, are you?" he asked, voice rough, like gravel in a dry riverbed. The boy nodded, sweat beading on his temple where the sun had baked the cotton too tight.  

The stranger stepped forward, boots crunching on the dust like stones breaking underfoot. "I seen that jacket before," he said, pointing at the one on the boy’s back. "Same one from the old saloon down by the creek. You been there, haven’ you?" Josh didn’t answer, just shifted his weight, one hand still resting on the boy’s shoulder, the other fiddling with the loose end of his rope belt. The boy felt it press into his ribs like a promise.  

A horse snorted from the shadow of the dry gulch, and the stranger’s eyes flicked to it—then back to the boy, slow and steady, like he was reading something written in the dust. "Guess you two oughta get movin’," he said, voice low. "That dust’s startin’ to rise like it’s got its own breath."

Tex didn’t answer right away, just let his breath catch in his throat like a man who’d seen a ghost. The stranger shifted again, slow and deliberate, and the couch creaked like an old horse’s back. Then he spoke, low and sharp, like a bullet that just missed its mark. “You don’t need to get up, Tex. You just need to *feel* it—like the wind in the canyon before the storm.”  

Tex exhaled, slow and heavy, and pulled his boots off one at a time, the soles scraping the floor like old tin. He didn’t look at the man, didn’t trust the silence, but his hands went to his belt, fingers working the leather until they found the edge of his duffel. The duffel was empty, except for a single rusted key and a half-eaten salami. He pulled it out, held it up in the dim light, and grunted. “I been lookin’ for that key since I got here. Thought it was in the barn. Thought it was in the preacher’s house.”  

The stranger didn’t move. Just let his ass press into the cushion like a man who’d been waiting too long, and Tex felt it—deep in his gut, the way a cold wind hits a dry canyon at dawn. He didn’t know where the key led, didn’t know if it opened a door or a grave, but he knew he had to move. And if the man didn’t answer when he called out, then he’d have to go find out.

Josh swallowed, hands still clutching the rope that had once tied the mule to the fence. The boy—now a boy with the weight of a hundred sunrises in his bones—looked at Gregory like he’d just seen a ghost of a man he’d once known. "You’re not the one who taught me how to ride," he said, voice rough, like he’d been scraping rust off a wagon wheel.  

Gregory didn’t answer. Just tilted his head, one ear twitching as if listening to the wind’s secret. Then he stepped forward, boots cracking the dust, and laid a hand on the boy’s shoulder. Not gentle. Not soft. Just like the way a man might tap a gun to see if it still worked. “You don’t need to be saved,” he said. “You just need to stop thinking you’re the only one who knows how to hold on.”  

The boy blinked. Then he looked at me, real quick, like he’d forgotten I was there. “I didn’t know you’d been waiting,” he said. “I thought you’d just… gone.” I didn’t answer. Just nodded, one corner of my lip twitching, like I’d seen a dog chew through a rope and still not realized how long it had been there. The wind picked up, carried with it the smell of old oil and something sour—like a tin can left in the sun too long.

The man grunted, shifted his weight, and slammed his fist into the saddle horn—hard enough to make the leather crack. "You talk like you been riding through the desert with a devil on your back," he said, wiping sweat from his brow with the back of his hand. "But this ain't just a ride. It’s a reckoning. You want passion? Then you better have a horse that’s been through a dust storm and still got its teeth in the ground."

He pulled the reins tight, kicked the mare once, and she stepped forward with a low snort, her hooves kicking up dust like a breath. "You said flat, furious, passionate," he growled, eyes locked on the other man’s. "So let’s see you do it—no fancy talk, no slow burn. Just you, me, and that horse like it’s the only thing left standing after the last roundup."

The wind picked up, not from the sky but from the ground—like the earth itself was stirring. The two men stood there, close, breathing hard, the saddle scraping against the dirt, and the sun still high, but now it felt like it was leaning in, watching.

The boy didn’t answer right away, just stood there, chest heaving, one hand fisted in the worn leather of the saddle, the other still pressed against the man’s hip. The sun had gone behind the ridge, and the sky was spilling copper and shadow, like oil on water. The man exhaled slow, a long breath that curled the air, and then he shifted, pulling the boy closer, boots scraping the dust as he moved. “You don’t have to stay quiet,” he said, voice low, “but you better not run again. Not till you know what it’s like to get caught in a storm with a man who knows your name.”

He turned the boy to face the trail, his hand still on the small of his back, and the boy felt it then—the way the man’s fingers dug into his flesh like roots finding soil. “I’ll ride you out past the ghost town,” he said, “and we’ll find that old corral where the wind still howls like a dog. You tell me if it’s still cold when you get there.”  

The boy nodded, jaw tight, eyes tracking the line of the road ahead. The wind picked up, snatching at the dust and the loose ends of their clothes. Somewhere past the cactus line, a lone horse whinnied, and the man didn’t flinch. He just let his thumb slide along the boy’s shoulder, slow and steady, like he was counting the seconds before the next thunder.

Trent kicked the dust off his boots and turned toward the stable, the old rusted gate groaning behind him like a dying dog. A silver flask clinked in his pocket—still warm from the fire, still full of whiskey he’d poured himself three days ago, before the fever hit. He didn’t see the shadow moving behind the haymow until he felt the weight of it, a hand on his shoulder, rough and sudden. “You left the saddle on the porch,” a voice said, dry as a cracked saddle, and Trent didn’t look back. “And the mule’s gone.”

He found the saddle half-buried under a tarp, the bridle chewed at the corners, the leather split like old skin. The mule wasn’t gone—she was standing near the creek, her tail twitching, one eye half-closed, the other blinking slowly. Trent stepped forward, boots sinking in the mud, and the mule snorted. Then she took a step, and the ground shifted beneath her hooves. The wind came up, not from the west, but from under the earth, like something had just stirred in the dark.  

Trent reached out, fingers brushing the saddle’s iron ring, and the flask slipped from his coat. He didn’t pick it up. He just stood there, watching the mule’s ear twitch once more, and the sky above turned the color of rusted steel.

Mitch grunted, one hand gripping the saddle horn like he was trying to pull the world back into place. The wind came in sharp through the chasm, carrying dust and the sour tang of dried sage. The cowboy’s knee pressed harder into the dirt, his breath ragged, and for a second Mitch thought he’d be carried off like a stray calf. Then the man pulled back, letting go of Mitch’s waist, and shoved his hands into the pockets of his jeans, fingers digging in.  

"Didn’t mean to go all slow," he said, voice rough as gravel, "but you were so still—like you’d been waiting for this all night."  

Mitch laughed, low and dry. "You just ain’t used to being held down, are you? Like a horse that’s been on a long trail and finally sees a well."  

The man nodded, eyes half-lidded, and with a grunt, he twisted, letting his weight shift forward so his shoulder pressed against Mitch’s ribs. The saddle creaked, the leather groaning like a tired old dog. The wind picked up again, and for a moment, the whole canyon seemed to hold its breath.

Joey grunted, one hand fumbling for the edge of the bedroll as he shifted, the fabric catching on his hip. “You’re not gonna make it out of this bedroll without a fight,” he said, voice thick with sweat and something else—something like shame or pride. Patsy laughed, a sharp, dry sound like a wind chime snapped in half, and hooked her finger under the collar of his shirt. “I ain’t asking for a fight, boy. Just a show. The sun’ll be up by the time you’re done.”  

She pulled him down further, the rough canvas scraping his back, and pressed her palm flat against the dip of his spine. “Now, don’t you go thinkin’ I’m some fancy gal with a silver flask and a lullaby. I’m just a woman who knows how to ride the heat and the silence like a horse knows its own trail.”  

Joey exhaled, slow and deep, and when he looked up, his eyes were half-lidded, the kind that saw things but didn’t quite believe they were real. “You got me,” he said. “But if I don’t come, it’s gonna be because you’re too damn close to the edge and I can’t tell if I’m still in the world or just dreaming it.”

Trent wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, eyes still glazed, and turned to the dusty trail ahead. "You think that's the only thing I need to get?" he said, voice rough. "I’ve got a saddle that’s been chewing on my hip for three days." He kicked at a loose stone, watching it roll into the hollow where the old windmill stood.  

Josh snorted, pulling his boots tighter. "You’re talkin’ about a saddle, but you’ve been drinkin’ that water from the dry well since the storm. That’s a problem, ain’t it?"  

A shadow passed over the ridge, and a horse snorted from the east. Trent didn’t look—didn’t need to. He knew the sound of that horse, knew the way it’d come up slow, like it was waiting for him to say something. Then, a voice from behind: "You still got that bottle of whiskey in your boot, don’t you?" It wasn’t a question. It was a fact, like the sun rising after a storm.  

Trent didn’t answer. Just turned, slow, and let the wind take his breath. The saddle creaked as he walked toward it, and for a moment, he thought he could still feel the heat of the thing in his mouth—like a brand on the inside of his jaw.

He didn’t move, just stayed there, chest heaving, fingers still curled in the sheets like he was afraid to let go. The boy’s breath still came in short, hot bursts, the wetness on his tongue still sticky as he tasted the salt of sweat and the copper of the boy’s come. Outside, the wind rattled the tin roof, and a dust devil rolled past the porch, kicking up a trail of yellow grit. 

"Damn," the man grunted, pushing himself up on one elbow, eyes squinting at the ceiling. "That’s the third time this week I’ve done it like that—no time to warm up, no time to think. Just… pulled it in and let it go." He reached for the lamp, flicked it on, and stared at the shadow of the boy’s legs still half-stretched out under the covers. "You ever think about what happens after?" 

He sat up fully now, the mattress groaning under the weight. The boy turned over slowly, one arm slipping off the bed, and the man reached down to grab his shoulder—rough, real, like a hand that hadn’t been polished by time or whiskey. "You know," he said, voice low, "I don’t care if you come back tomorrow or not. Just don’t come back without telling me where you went."

The boy exhaled, slow and deep, like he’d been holding his breath since the first gunshot cracked the night air. His fingers curled into the cotton of the bedroll, knuckles white, and that’s when the sheriff saw it—the smear of dried blood on the inside of the boy’s sleeve, not from a wound, but from where he’d scraped his arm on the rusted rail during the last hold-up. The boy hadn’t been running from nothing. He’d been running from something that still clung to the saddle.

“Didn’t think you’d make it back,” the sheriff muttered, voice low, like he was talking to the wind and the wind didn’t care. “Didn’t think you’d be standing here, barefoot in the dust, with that same kind of look in your eye.” The boy shifted, slow, and the heat between them didn’t vanish—it just changed, thickened, like the oil in the engine after a long ride.

The sheriff reached out then, not to touch, but to pull the boy’s hand up, palm down, and let it rest on the cold iron of the boot heel. “You don’t need to grow anymore,” he said. “Just keep your hands steady.” And for a second, the boy didn’t move, didn’t speak, and the silence between them was full of things unsaid—like the name of a town, or the way the wind used to whistle in the dry creek bed.

Mitch’s fingers slipped past the collar, snagging the thread where it’d been stitched too tight, and he gave a sharp tug, the fabric pulling like a yoke. “You top or being sir?” he repeated, voice low, a little rough from the sweat and the way the sun had baked the dust into his skin. The man across the table didn’t answer right away—just stared at the poker in his hand, the blackened end still smoking.  

Then he leaned forward, slow and deliberate, and knocked the poker into the tin plate beside him. The sound cracked like a dry branch splitting in the wind. “Top,” he said, and it wasn’t a joke. “I top. You just keep your hands off my back, and don’t let the wind blow through your hair when you’re talkin’.”  

Mitch laughed, a dry, rattling sound, and reached under the table, fingers brushing the old revolver tucked beneath the napkin. “I’ll keep my hands on you,” he said, “but only if you promise not to take off your boots till we get to the next stage.”

He shifted, rolling onto his side, the mattress groaning like an old wagon under a heavy load. Darlis wiped his lips with the back of his hand and looked at the other man’s face—still half-shadowed in the dim light, eyes half-lidded, breath slow. “You ain’t gotta say it,” he said, voice rough. “Just let me know when you feel it. When you know it’s real.”  

The man exhaled, a long, slow pull of air that made the room feel colder than before. “I feel it,” he said, not looking at Darlis. “Like the wind hits the ridge after a storm. Like the dirt’s still wet under the horses’ hooves.”  

Then he turned, pressing his shoulder into Darlis’s, and the silence between them wasn’t empty anymore—just thick with the kind of quiet that comes when two men know they’ve been waiting for something that doesn’t need words. The cold hadn’t done it. It was the stillness. The way the clock on the wall ticked like a heartbeat. And for the first time, Darlis didn’t care if it was too late. He just wanted to feel the shift, the way one man’s body might finally meet another’s without any kind of promise left unsaid.

The horse snorted, pawing at the dry earth like it wanted to charge into the dust and ride off with the heat still burning in its bones. The young man groaned again, not from pain but from the way the world had narrowed to just that one spot between them—hot, tight, alive—and the way the air smelled of sweat and dry sage, of old gunpowder and something older, something buried in the ground.  

The man on top didn’t stop, didn’t even shift, just pressed harder, each stroke dragging the back of his hand across the young man’s shoulder like a warning or a promise. “You’re gonna come like you did in the old days,” he growled, voice raw, “when the trail was long and the sky cracked like a dry pie.”  

Then the young man’s arm slipped free and landed flat on the saddle horn, his breath ragged, eyes half-lidded, as if he’d seen something in the distance that wasn’t there—just a flicker of shadow moving past the timber line, a shape like a man with a gun, standing still like he’d been waiting for this moment to happen.

The wind snatched the last of the brand paint off the fence post, and the cowboy shoved a hand into his coat, pulling out a rusted pocketknife. "That’s right," he said, tapping the blade against the pitted metal. "You don’t need a bond to know a man’s blood. You just gotta feel it run under your skin like a line of fire."  

Jonah groaned, half-sitting on the barrel, one leg still dangling over the edge like a dog after a fight. His boots were scuffed, his shirt torn at the shoulder, and he didn’t move when the cowboy slid the knife into the dirt, then turned it over. "I seen a man once, back in Laramie, who used to carry a silver spoon like a weapon. Said it was the only thing that didn’t lie. Well, I didn’t believe him till I saw the spoon in the dust after a storm, still warm."  

The cowboy grinned, his eyes catching the sun between the dry timber. "Now you know what it feels like to be seen, don’t you?" And he leaned in, close enough that Jonah could smell the sweat and the dust, and the quiet hum of something old and real, like a horse after a long trail.

The bed creaked under the weight of his hip, the mattress groaning like an old horse in a dry wind. He didn’t answer right away—just kept his eyes on the other man’s shoulder, watching the way the muscle twitched under the cotton shirt. "Marinating?" the other one said, voice dry like a cracked pan. "You mean like a steak in the sun? That’s not how it works. You don’t cook it slow and pretend it’ll never taste like meat."  

He shifted, pulling the man’s arm down so his fingers brushed the edge of the blanket. "You don’t *want* it to last, you just want to believe it can. Like a promise you made to a ghost." A pause. Then, with a grunt, he pushed himself up, one hand on the frame, the other digging into the man’s waist. "Now let’s see if you’ve got the grit to take a real ride."  

The wind came in through the cracked window, carrying dust and the smell of burned sage from the next county. The man didn’t move. Just let the weight of the moment settle, like a saddle settling on a bad back.

He grunted, pushing his boots off the floor with a thud, the leather cracking like old bone. “Wanted to get in the saddle before sundown, that’s all. Ain’t got nothin’ to do with the wind or the way the sun bleeds over the hills.”  

She snorted, tossing the sheet onto the bed like a dead leaf. “You think I don’t know what you’re really after? You want to ride into that dust and leave the whole damn town behind like a man who’s run out of money and prayers.”  

He reached for his coat, pulled it on over his shirt, and paused. “Well, I’ll be back with a story or two, maybe a dead man’s boot or two. Either way, I’ll be riding east, not west. That’s what I’ve decided.”  

The lantern flickered, casting long shadows that looked like hands reaching from the wall. Outside, a horse snorted, and the wind carried the smell of dry clay and something sharp—like rust, or old blood.

He pulled back just enough to catch the edge of the man’s jacket, the one with the frayed brass button, and spat into the dirt. "Yeah, I do. That’s why I’m still standing here with a rifle in one hand and a busted saddle in the other." The sun beat down hard on the cracked earth, the kind of heat that made a man sweat through his shirt even when he didn’t move.  

“Saddle’s got a crack down the side,” the other said, voice rough as a chisel, “like it was chewed by a mule.”  

"Could be," the first man muttered, wiping his mouth with the back of his hand. "Or could be a ghost riding it."  

He stepped sideways, kicked a stone loose from the cinder block fence, and the sound cracked like a dry bone. The wind didn’t shift, but for a second the dust smelled like burnt hay and old oil—like something had just gone wrong in the stable behind the saloon.  

No one spoke. Just watched the dust settle. The silence was thick enough to chew.

The boy’s breath hitched, slow and deep, like a horse after a long run. He didn’t move, just stared at the sheriff’s boots kicked into the dirt, one toe curled like a warning. The wind snatched the dust from the saddle and spat it back at the man’s face—sharp, stinging, like a warning he’d been waiting for.  

“You still got that old Colt in your hip pocket?” the sheriff said, not looking up.  

“Yessir,” the man grunted, fumbling it out. The gun was cold, the barrel dented where it’d been jammed in a saloon fight two years back. He pulled it down and tapped it twice on the boy’s shoulder. “That’s the one that saved your life, kid. Not the one you’re gonna need to get out of this town with.”  

The boy blinked, then reached under his coat and pulled out a silver locket, open now—inside, a faded photo of a woman with a red hat and a dog that looked like a terrier with too many wrinkles. He didn’t say anything. Just let the wind carry the silence between them like a dry, unbroken rope.

The man with the sun-bleached hat stepped into the saloon, boots scraping the dirt floor, and tossed a folded letter onto the bar. "That's the one," he said, pointing at a stack of maps beside the whiskey bottle. "Drew's got the trail at the bend—no one’s seen the herd since last moonrise. If the boys go in there with the wagons, they’ll be stuck in the sand like a busted horse in a storm."

He pulled a rusted silver key from his coat pocket and held it up like a torch. "This one’s from the old rancher's daughter. Said it opened the gate behind the stone wall. Not a lock, not a gate—just a crack in the earth, like the land itself had a tooth and bit in." The bartender squinted. "You sure it ain’t just a joke from some drunk with a bad dream?"

The young man at the table, one hand on a shotgun, nodded. "I’m not chasing ghosts. I’m chasing a herd that ain’t supposed to be there. And if it runs, it runs straight through the dry creek bed where the old man used to dig wells and never filled them." He tapped the key against the wood. "This’ll open the gate. And maybe, just maybe, it’ll let the wind go back to blowing the right way."

Darrin didn’t wait for an answer. He slid his hand under the collar of the man’s shirt, fingers pressing into the soft flesh of his shoulder. The other man didn’t flinch, just shifted a little, like he’d been waiting for that touch. “You’re a damn good liar,” he said, voice low, “but you don’t have to lie to me. I seen you in the saloon last week, with that kid from the north—same shirt, same smirk. You were holding a glass of bourbon like it was a promise.”

“Him?” The man laughed, a dry, rattling sound. “He was just trying to look tough. You don’t get a man like that, not with a face like that and a jaw that doesn’t move unless it’s been told to.” He stepped back, eyes flicking to the rusted gate behind them, where a black horse stood still, head low, one hoof tapping like a metronome.

“Still think you’re the sexy faggot?” Darrin asked, leaning back now, arms folded. “Or just the one who’s got the nerve to wear his pride like a badge?”

Trent didn’t move. Just stood there in the pale light, one hand still on the cold metal of the shower handle, the other still half-dripping from where he’d just scrubbed his face. The water had stopped. The sound of the pipe hissing behind the wall was all that broke the silence now. Jesse stared at him, not quite sure if he was seeing the boy or remembering him.  

“Your desk?” Jesse said, voice rough. “You felt me from your desk?”  

Trent nodded, slow as a plow through mud. “Like a spark. Like a wire run through the floor. I didn’t even know I was sitting when it happened. Just… felt it. Like something warm pressing into the back of my skull.”  

Jesse stepped forward, boots scuffing the linoleum, and looked down at the boy’s bare arms—thin, scarred from a bad fall on the old sawmill. “You didn’t even know you were there,” he said, and laughed, low and dry. “Well, now you know. And I’m starting to think the whole damn town’s been humming since the night the wind stopped.”

I spit a chunk of tobacco into the dust and wiped my hands on my jeans. "Yeah, well, I didn’t know it then, not really. But I seen you two in that back room, the one with the cracked floorboard—dirt like a griddle in the corner. You been talking about the feel of it, like it was a kind of prayer. I thought you were just trying to impress me, but you were feelin’ it. Like the ground was shakin’ under your boots when you came back out, sweat on your collar, eyes hollowed out."

He leaned on the porch rail, boots caked with mud, and looked at me like I’d just said something true. "You ever feel that way when you’re drunk and the sun’s low, and you’re out west and you don’t know if you’re livin’ or just waitin’ for the wind to take you?" I didn’t answer. Just nodded, eyes on the dirt where a horse’s hoof had left a smear. "Then you know what I mean. The way it changes you—like the world don’t matter no more, just the ache in your gut and the way your bones hum when you walk."

I pulled my hat low and stepped into the shadow of the old fence. The wind picked up, and for a second, the sound of a bull coughin’ from the ridge made it feel like the whole damn valley was breathin’. Then the dust settled and I said, "So you think it was more than just fuckin’? That it was… a kind of truth?" I didn’t wait for him to answer. Just kept walking, boots crunchin’ on the dry bones of last year’s fence posts.

Mitch lunged forward, hand snapping out to grab the man’s shoulder, but the stranger was already twisting away, a half-smile playing at his lips. "You ain’t got a gun, boy," he said, voice smooth as oil, "but you got that look in your eyes—like you’ve seen the devil in a mirror and he’s still breathing."  

The man pulled a cigarette from his vest, lit it with a spark from his pocket, and held it between two fingers like a piece of meat. The smoke curled into the dusty air, and for a second, the room smelled like burnt bone and old boots. Mitch didn’t flinch. He just stood there, jaw tight, watching the man take a slow drag, then exhale, the ghost of a laugh slipping past his lips.  

"Name’s Jax," the stranger said, pointing at the floor where a loose plank creaked underfoot. "You know that place down by the old windmill? Where the water’s always runnin’ low?" Mitch nodded. "Well, that’s where I found your horse yesterday—dead, but not yet buried. And your boots, still on. Like you’d been runnin’ through the dust all night, only you didn’t come back."

The old man coughed, spit a chunk of rust-colored blood into the dust, and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "Yours, too, ain't it?" he said, voice gravelly as a cracked boot heel. "You get that deep in the ground, you don’t know what’s real and what’s just the wind playin’ tricks."  

He leaned back on the saddle horn, hands on the cold iron of the rifle, and watched the dust swirl around the hollow where the wind had just blown out a man’s breath. A shadow passed over the cattail fence, and the young man at the end of the line turned—no, not turned, just shifted, like he’d been standing there waiting for the silence to crack.  

"Guess you're still in the middle of it," the old man muttered, looking down at the hump of a saddle bag that had spilled open. Inside, a dried leather boot lay half-buried in the dirt, one heel missing. "Like the world’s just a damn dream that won't let go."

The cowboy pulled back just enough to look down at the boy’s face, eyes half-lidded, sweat streaking his brow. “You think you’re the only one who’s been good?” he growled, thumb brushing the boy’s jaw. “You don’t even know what you’ve done, do you? You’ve been hauling water from the creek at dawn, fixin’ the wagon when the rain came, stayin’ up past sundown to watch the line of dust roll down the ridge—like you owed me something.”  

He shifted, his boot pressing into the dirt, and the boy’s hands slipped to his hips, fingers tightening. “I seen you in the stable, sittin’ on the cold floor with the mules, readin’ that old book you never let me borrow. You were quiet then, like you didn’t want to say no. And now you’re here, breathin’ heavy, like you’re scared to say it out loud.”  

The cowboy exhaled, slow and deep, then reached behind him and yanked the belt of his own pants free. “You’re not goin’ back to that little town in the valley, not with the dust in your boots and the sun in your eyes. You’re stayin’ right here. And I’m gonna make you forget what it’s like to be alone.”

Trent caught the edge of the porch step and kicked it once, hard, sending a chip flying into the dust. The silence wasn’t just quiet—it was thick, like oil on a hot pan. He turned to see Mitch’s dad standing in the shadows, one hand in his coat, the other tapping the porch rail like he was counting the seconds. “You two done?” he asked, not looking at either of them.  

“Still breathing,” Mitch said, grinning, “but the fire’s gone cold.” He reached into his pocket and pulled out a folded piece of paper—half-burned at the edges. “I found this in the back of the barn. Looks like a map. Or a list. Names, maybe. All scratched in pencil.”  

Trent looked at it, then at the ground. “Like the names of the men who died in that fight back in ’37?” He didn’t wait for an answer. Just kept walking, boots crunching on gravel, the way a man walks when he knows something’s wrong and doesn’t know what it is yet.

The cowboy grunted, shifted his weight, and let his boot heel dig into the dust just past the old windmill. The boy’s hands were still curled in the reins, fingers white, but he didn’t move. Just watched, like a pup waiting to be called. "You ain’t got to say nothing," the cowboy rumbled, voice rough as gravel in a dry creek. "Just let the air taste like rust and smoke, and the dirt smell like old blood."  

He pulled the boy’s coat tighter, the fabric scraping the boy’s shoulders. "You think I’m the only one who’s ever been hanged in a dream?" The boy didn’t laugh, but his jaw twitched. "I seen a man once, down in the canyon, swingin’ from a fence post like a rusted hook. Said he was tryin’ to reach the sky, but all he got was a scratch and a taste of wind."  

The cowboy let out a long breath and turned his head, one eye scanning the ridge where the sun dipped low like a drunk man’s hand. "Now I’m here, and you’re still hangin’ on like a prayer," he said. "And I don’t even know if I’m prayin’ for you or just wantin’ to feel your skin burnin’ through the wool."

He gritted his teeth and shoved forward, the boy’s spine arching like a bowstring, and the cowboy groaned, not from pain but from the way the heat of it spilled through the leather of his pants. The door creaked shut behind them—no one had noticed, not the cook on the porch, not the dog barking at the wind—just the way the oil lamp flickered and the mirror reflected a smear of sweat and red dust on the boy’s cheek.

"Damn it, I thought I was gonna make it out of this thing with a clean shirt," he muttered, rolling onto his side, one hand still pressed into the boy’s hip. The boy didn’t move, just exhaled, slow and deep, like he’d been holding it since the first time he’d seen the range lights come on.  

The cowboy kicked the edge of the sink, sending a splash of water into the sink, then reached for the towel on the hook—stained, frayed at the ends, the kind you’d find in a saloon after a fight. He wiped his face, then looked down at the boy’s hand, still curled around the edge of the toilet. “You ever seen a man get choked by a horse?” he asked, not expecting an answer. The boy just nodded, slow, like he was still listening to something beneath the floorboards.

Josh shifted on the bed, one hand still pressed into the mattress where the sheets had been pulled up, the other tightening around the edge of the quilt. “You’re right,” he said, voice rough, like it had been scraped by dust and wind. “I didn’t want you to go. Not after that first time. Like I was already halfway in, and you were still pulling me back in.” He sat up a little, looking at Jonah with that slow, patient gaze again—like he’d been waiting for the right moment to say it, and now it had come.  

Jonah exhaled, a long, slow breath, and then laughed—dry, sharp, like a nail scraping wood. “You think I didn’t know you were holding back?” he said, eyes narrowing. “I seen the way you kept your hands still when I pulled you down. Like you were afraid to move too fast.” He reached out and tapped Josh’s forearm, just once, hard enough to make the skin tingle. “So now you want me to do it again? Like a damn circus act? You want me to go down on you, just to prove I can still make you come?”  

Josh didn’t answer right away. Just stared at the ceiling, his boots still laced tight, his boots still dusty from the trail. Then he said, “I don’t need you to prove it. I just need you to stay. Like you were when I was scared, when the wind was howling and the sun was low and the world felt like it was about to split.”

Darrin’s hand slid down to the small of his partner’s back, fingers pressing just hard enough to make him shiver. “You think I’m a faggot?” he said, low and rough, voice catching on the word like a dry stone in a boot. “Then you oughta see the way that old mule in the corral still whimpers when I saddle her.”  

The man shifted, shoulders rolling back as if trying to straighten out the ache in his spine. “Yeah, I seen that,” he said, eyes narrowing. “But you ain’t got the patience of a man who’s ever been in a fight for his life.”  

A shadow passed across the roof of the bunkhouse—no wind, just the sun slanting through the cracked eaves. Darr’s boots tapped a beat against the floorboards, slow and steady, like a man counting breaths before he speaks again. “Then maybe I ain’t a faggot,” he said, “but I am a man who knows how to make a woman cry when she thinks she’s been left behind.”

The boy groaned low, teeth pressing into the flesh of the cowboy’s shoulder, and the saddle leather creaked as he shifted, one hand slipping down to grip the rail. The sun still burned through the dust, painting the sagebrush red and sharp. The cowboy didn’t look up, just kept his eyes on the boy’s, watching the way his jaw worked, the way the sweat glistened on his neck like oil.

"Keep movin’," he said, voice rough, "like you're makin' the earth move." The boy pulled back just enough to catch a breath, then slid back in, deeper, and the sound of their bodies grinding together was like stones scraping on a dry riverbed. The boy’s fingers curled into the cowboy’s shirt, and for a second, the world went still—just the two of them, the heat, the smell of horse sweat and wet earth.

The cowboy exhaled and kicked the horse’s flank, hard, sending it snorting and rearing just enough to swing the boy’s leg over the saddle. "You ain’t got no time to waste," he growled, "not when the trail’s half a mile off and the wind’s pickin’ up." The boy didn’t answer, just let his head fall back, eyes half-lidded, one hand still clamped tight on the cowboy’s arm. The sky cracked with a sudden thunderclap, and the dust lifted like a wave, washing over them both.

Jessier didn’t flinch when Josh slammed the door behind him, boots caked in dust from the old trail behind the saloon. She was barefoot, hair tied back with a strip of oilskin, one hand wrapped around a rusted poker, the other curled around the edge of the bed. “You said you’d stay,” she said, voice low, like she was used to the silence of a dry wind.

Josh wiped the sweat from his brow with the back of his hand, not looking at her. “I did. But the way that damn toy sucked the oil from the sheriff’s boots, like it was hungry—” He stopped, looked at her. “You know what that means, don’t you?”

Jessier nodded, slow, eyes steady. “Means the sheriff’s not coming back from the mesa, and the boys down at the dry well are already singing his name in the dark.” She stepped forward, the poker clanging against the wood. “So you’re not gonna tell me what you really wanted to say when you left the tent, are you?”

The boy’s ass twitched under the weight of the sheriff’s thick shaft, the leather of his saddle bag scraping against the dried mud where the buckboard had stalled. The cowboy didn’t flinch—he just tightened his grip on the reins, boots digging into the dirt like a man trying to hold on to something that wasn’t there. The sheriff groaned low, a sound like gravel in a tin can, and shifted, pushing deeper into the boy’s flesh with a slow, deliberate drag.

"Easy, boy," the sheriff rasped, voice rough as old rope, "you don’t have to be all slick and still like a wet hound. Just let the heat run through you." The cowboy watched the way the boy’s hands fumbled with the frayed edge of his shirt, fingers brushing the nape of his neck like he was trying to find a prayer in the dust. The wind picked up, snatching at the loose end of the sheriff’s hat, and for a second, it looked like the whole damn valley was holding its breath.

Then the boy let out a sharp exhale, and the sheriff’s cock pulsed again—this time not just heat, but a kind of quiet, steady throb that made the cowboy feel the ground shift beneath him. The boy didn’t move, didn’t even flinch, just stared at the sky where a lone hawk circled, wings spread wide like a question mark. The cowboy shifted his weight, his boots creaking, and knew—something was going to break, but not yet. Not until the silence turned into something else.

Josh pulled back just enough to see the boy’s breath catch, then slammed his hand on the saddle horn, hard. "You thinkin’ I’m gonna let you ride off with the sun still up?" he growled, the words rough as gravel. The boy grinned, teeth chipped from a night of chewing on rusted nails, and said, "Only if you promise not to tell anyone about the time you faked a fever to get the doctor to come in early."  

Josh snorted, then reached down and tugged the boy’s coat collar up, rough fingers tracing the line of his neck. "I remember that. You was three days overdue, and I was sick as a dog, fevered to the bone. I told the doc I’d been laid up since the last rodeo. Said I couldn’t even stand up straight. He came in with a bottle of whiskey and a pair of boots, and you stood there in your boots, looking like you'd seen a ghost."  

The boy shifted, one hand curling into the leather of the saddle, the other brushing the nape of Josh’s neck. "You still had the boots," he said, quiet now, like he didn’t want to break the stillness. "And you wore them in the rain. Right after the storm hit."

Josh didn’t move, just watched the way Silver’s boots kicked the dust in slow, deliberate arcs. The boy’s shirt was still half-tucked, one sleeve torn at the elbow like it’d been chewed by a rusted hinge. Silver’s hand came down on the boy’s shoulder, not hard—just enough to make the flesh hum—then he leaned close, breath hot on the back of Josh’s neck. “You don’t gotta be proud of it, you know,” he said, voice rough as gravel in a dry creek. “Just gotta know when to stop.”  

The boy shifted, pulled his hand back from the wall like he was trying to catch a shadow. A flicker of something sharp passed between them—something older than the fight, older than the way the porch sagged under the weight of the world. “You think I’m not done yet?” Josh asked, and didn’t wait for a reply. He stepped forward, hands open like he was offering a gun that hadn’t fired yet.  

Silvers coughed, wiped his thumb over the edge of his boot. “I think you’re just waiting for me to say something real.” And then he did, low and slow: “Tell me where you’d go if you had to run.” The boy didn’t answer right away. Just stared at the spot where the floor met the wall, like it might speak.

He gritted his teeth and shifted, pressing harder into the curve of the man’s back, the ache in his shoulder flaring like a spark. "Not raw, honey," he growled, "just honest. Like a saddle that’s been ridden too long—gives out where it's supposed to hold."  

The other man didn’t answer right away. Just let his hands slide down to the small of his back, fingers digging into the loose fabric of his shirt. Then he pulled him back, hard, and whispered, “Then let it break.”  

A low chuckle came from the corner of the room, like a windmill creaking in a dust storm. “You two sound like you been spilling oil on the porch,” said a voice from the shadows. “I seen the horses in the corral, and they don’t even make a sound when they’re tired.”  

The man on the bed didn’t move. Just let his breath catch, slow and deep, like he was waiting for something to happen that hadn’t yet. The night didn’t care. It just kept stretching, warm and full, like a blanket left too long on a sleeping man.

The boy didn’t flinch, just shifted his weight back, letting the sheriff’s shoulder press harder into his spine. A grizzled hand patted the boy’s shoulder, slow and heavy like a wagon wheel turning on rusted axles. “You ever been to the old saloon down by the creek?” the sheriff asked, voice rough as cracked leather. “The one with the tin roof and the bell that never rings?”  

The boy grunted, pulled his shirt down over his hips. “That place’s been gutted since ’37. Dust in the corners like old bones.”  

“Then you know what they say,” the sheriff said, eyes scanning the cracked pavement, “if you ain’t got a name, you ain’t got nothin’. And if you ain’t got nothin’, you’re just a ghost with a rifle.”  

He pushed off, straightened, and gave the boy a look that didn’t quite leave the heat of the moment—like he’d been drinking from a canteen too long and just couldn’t remember how to stop. “Now, you tell me, what’s your name, son?”  

The boy didn’t answer right away. Just looked past the sheriff, at the sun dipping low behind the dry sagebrush, and let his hands rest on the cold iron of his belt.

Darrin’s fingers curled into Dare’s shirt, rough and dusty, and the scent of sweat and old horsehide hit him like a slap. He didn’t lean in yet—no, not till he felt the weight of Dare’s breath on his neck, hot and steady. The silence cracked when Dare pulled back just enough to look at him, eyes wide, pupils like blackened coals. “You ain’t got nothin’ to lose,” he said, voice raw, like it had been scraped clean by the wind. “Not since you came in here with that damn rifle and that smile.”

Scott exhaled, slow and deep, and shifted his weight. “You two still talkin’ about what’s behind the saloon?” he asked, squinting at the cracked mirror above the bar, where a silver locket dangled loose. “I seen it, that one. The one with the woman’s face carved in the back.” His hands trembled slightly as he reached for it, fingers brushing the cold metal. “Like it was buried in the dust, and just waited for someone to find it.”

Dare didn’t answer right away. Just stared at the locket, then at Darrin, and for a second, the room felt like it had shrunk to the size of a saddle horn. Then he said, “I found it when I was cleaning the barn. It wasn’t meant to be found. It was meant to be *remembered*.”

The door slammed behind him, rattling the loose board on the wall, and Darr’lin grunted, his hips jerking like a winded horse. “Damn it, boy, you’re not even dressed like a man yet and you’ve got me half-erect again,” he muttered, pushing back into Gregory’s frame with a grunt. “Saw that old barn door swingin’ when you came in—must’ve been a full moon, or you’da missed the smell of the dry grass and the sweat in the air.”  

Gregory gasped, hand slipping to the back of Darrin’s neck, fingers tightening. “I was just lookin’ for the lantern,” he said, voice rough, “but I saw your boots in the mud, and your hat tipped sideways like it was fightin’ the wind.” His breath hitched as Darrin pulled back, then drove forward again, slow and heavy, like a plow through dust.  

The porch swing creaked, and a shadow moved across the floorboards—old Man Harkins, leaning on his walking stick, his coat flapping like a banner. “You two still playin’ with the light of the world?” he called, not smiling. “Or just waitin’ for the next one to come?”

Mitch’s hand slipped into the pocket of his worn jeans and pulled out a crumpled piece of paper—half-burnt at the edges, the ink smudged like old sweat. “Guess I’m not the only one who’s been runnin’ from a preacher’s ghost,” he said, tossing it into the saddlebag. “Y’know, the one who showed up on the church porch with a six-shooter and a hymnbook, said he was the last of the lost saints.”  

He grinned again, this time a little wider, eyes tracking the dust trail behind the old wagon as it groaned past the saloon. “Went right after the preacher died, you see. Found a ledger in the wall—numbers in blood, names of men who’d never been named in the records. One of ‘em was me, but I didn’t know it until the whiskey tasted like rust.”  

The wind snatched a loose ribbon from his hat, flung it over the fence like a warning, and the young man on the far side of the track just laughed, sharp and sudden, like a bullet hitting dry wood.

Trent dropped the flask into the saddlebag with a thud, wiped his hands on his pants, and stomped the dust from his boots. The saloon door swung open just as he reached the horse, a red-streaked mare with one eye gone bad, and a man in a greasy hat stepped out with a suitcase full of broken tinware. "You got that right," he said, grinning like he’d seen a ghost. "I’m the one who sold the old man his last bottle of brandy. That’s how he died, you know—sipped it down like a prayer."  

He didn’t wait for a reply. Just turned and walked toward the corrals, boots clacking on the gravel like a metronome counting down. Trent pulled the reins tight, the mare snorting as if it knew something had shifted. A shadow passed over the bar, and a girl with a black scarf wrapped around her neck stepped out from behind the counter, eyes wide, fingers tapping the wood. “You ever see a man with two left hands and a heart full of lies?” she asked, voice low. “That’s what I saw when I looked in the mirror.”  

Trent didn’t answer. Just kept walking, the wind tugging at his coat, the sun low and hot behind the ridge, the dust rising like a warning. The mare snorted again, this time with a long, shuddering breath. Then she turned and trotted past the old well, where a rusted bell hung by a frayed rope, and the sound of it chimed once, slow and hollow—like someone had just stopped talking.

Dare didn’t move, just stood there, dripping, the water still running in a thin, lazy stream down his back. The cowboy wiped his hands on his jeans and stepped back, boots caked with mud from the trail, like he’d just come from a fight with the wind. “You think I’m some kind of saint?” he asked, leaning against the sink, eyes on the mirror. “I’ve been down in the canyon where the river’s dry and the sun bleeds red. I’ve seen men die and women cry in the dark, and I still come back to this place like it’s a promise.”  

The bathroom light flickered again, and for a second, the mirror showed two men—not Dare and the cowboy, but two silhouettes standing on opposite ends of a long, dusty road. Then the hum came again, deeper this time, a vibration in the floorboards. It wasn’t a sound, not exactly—more like the ground breathing. The cowboy turned, eyes sharp, and said, “You ever hear a curre that don’t belong to a place? One that sings when you’re not looking?”  

Dare blinked. “I heard it last night,” he said, voice rough. “When I was asleep. Like a horse coughing in the middle of a storm.” The cowboy didn’t answer right away. Just stared at the floor, where a crack ran like a line of blood, and then he stepped forward, slow, hands still on the cold metal of the sink, and said, “Then you know it’s not just the land that’s waiting. It’s you.”

The sun was still hot on the dust, but the air had shifted—thicker, like the kind that comes after a man’s sweat has dried on the saddle. He spat into the dirt, the flecks of red in the grit catching the light, and said, “Yeah, I do. I ain’t got time for fancy talk when the wind’s blowin’ through the cattail patch and the coyotes’re startin’ to howl.”  

He pulled the Colt from the saddle horn, checked the hammer, then slapped it twice on the leather seat. “Saw that rusted wagon come in last night—same one that broke in the dry wash. That’s the one that got the kid from the east side. Didn’t even get to the porch before the horse bolted.”  

A shadow passed across the fence line. “You ever seen a man ride a horse like that, only it’s not the horse that’s off balance—it’s the rider. Like he’s tryin’ to walk through the air.” The voice was quiet, low, like it’d been chewing on a dry biscuit all day.  

He didn’t look back, just turned his head to where the wind carried the smell of wet feed and old blood. The sun was still hot, but the silence had deepened—like the earth had stopped breathing.

Tex didn’t wait for an answer. He grabbed the oil can from the table and sloshed a good half cup into his palm, then rubbed it between his hands until it shimmered like wet copper. The smell hit Jameson first—hot metal and burned oil—and he flinched, then groaned again, like a man remembering a bad dream.  

He didn’t say anything, just let the warmth spread through his shoulders as Tex began to work the chain across his back, slow and deliberate. The metal bit into the skin at first, then settled, like a second layer of bone. Jameson’s breath came in sharp bursts, each one dragging the air like a dry rope.  

“Still holding on, ain’t ya?” Tex said, his voice low, almost a growl, as he shifted the chain just a little to the left. Jameson didn’t answer. Just let his head fall back, one hand gripping the arm of the chair like a lifeline, the other twitching as if trying to keep the chain from slipping into his spine.

The boy gasped, hand clamping down on the armrest like he’d been slapped. "You mean to say it wasn’t just the music? That it wasn’t the rhythm, the way the fiddle cut through the dust and the lights flickered like a dying campfire?"  

The cowboy grunted, shifted his weight, and pulled the boy closer—no need for words now, just the scrape of leather against denim, the way the air between them thickened with sweat and the smell of old boots. "I didn’t want to take it, not really," he said, voice low, like he was telling a ghost. "But when the singer started singing that lullaby, the whole room stopped breathing. And I knew—knew—there was no turning back."  

The boy’s fingers twitched on the seat, then curled into fists. "Then what? You just… stayed?"  

"Stayed," the cowboy said, and his hand found the boy’s waist, fingers tightening just enough to make the bones vibrate. "Like the old ones did. Like they always did."

He took a step back, boots scuffing the dust like a man who’d just stepped out of a storm. “Me,” he said, voice rough, “I had to stay. The saloon’s on fire and the landlord’s gone blind from fever, so I’m still running the books. That’s what I do—keep the place turning, even when the roof’s leaking and the law’s got no name.” He looked at Mitch, eyes narrowed, one hand on the handle of his Colt. “You think I’d let you go off with a horse and a dead man’s hat and not see what’s really going on?”

Mitch didn’t answer right away. Just stood there, one foot tapping slow on the cracked tile, like he was counting the breaths in a dying man’s chest. Then he said, “So you stayed because you had to. Not because you wanted to.”  

A slow grin cracked his face. “Yeah. And you stayed ‘cause you didn’t know how to leave.”

Scott didn’t breathe till the man’s boots hit the gravel and the shadow stretched long and thin across the porch. The stranger stood there, jaw tight, one hand shoved in the pocket of his jeans, the other curled around a rusted crowbar. No words. Just that stare—like he’d been waiting for the world to stop turning so he could finally step into it.

“You’re the one who took the horse from the corral last night,” Scott said, voice low, gravelly, like he’d been chewing on the edge of a saddle for days. “Didn’t say a word. Just walked up, grabbed it, and left it in the mud.”

The man didn’t blink. “I saw you watching the tracks. You knew I was coming. You just didn’t know I’d be back.”

Scott stepped forward, his boots scraping the wood, and for a second the heat in his chest didn’t roar—it stuttered, like a broken engine. Then he reached out and pulled the crowbar from the man’s hand, the metal clinking, sharp. “You don’t have to explain. Just tell me what you’re going to do with it.”  

He didn’t wait for an answer. The man’s eyes went wide, then narrowed, and Scott saw it—the same flicker in the shadow, the same pulse in the air. Like the city had just let go of its breath.

The boy didn’t flinch, just shifted his weight, letting the weight of the man’s body press into his lower back like a wet blanket. The room smelled of old oil and sweat, the kind that clung to a man after a long ride through dust. The man’s hand slipped from the boy’s shoulder and found the small of his back, fingers digging in just enough to make the boy breathe slow.

"Can’t you tell I’m not tryin’ to get you to come?" the man muttered, voice rough as a saddle rope. "I’m just hangin’ here, like a dead man on a fence post, waitin’ for the wind to blow the dust off my boots again." He pulled the boy’s arm, not gently, and the boy stumbled forward, feet catching on the edge of a rusted tin bucket.  

A loud *clank* echoed, like a bell struck in a dry canyon. The boy looked down and saw the bucket was open, spilling a heap of dry, crinkled letters — all stamped with the same faded red wax: *For the Sheriff, by the River*. One of them fluttered to the floor, caught on a nail, and fluttered like a moth.

The sheriff pulled his hat low, fingers tracing the bristle of a stubbled jaw, and looked at the old rusted poker still smoldering in the corner of the saloon. "I was in the canyon when she first called out — blood in the water, the wind smelling like burnt meat. Didn’t know then that the girl was already gone, or that the body was buried under a stack of hay in the back of the stable." He tapped the poker with his boot. "Thought it was just a bad dream. Then the next day, the preacher said the same thing — saw a woman in the smoke, standing over the well with a lantern in her hand. Said she wasn’t human, but the way she looked at the men, like they were already dead, that was the sign."

He set the poker down and turned to the boy who'd been waiting with a flask of whiskey. "You know what I found in the stable, right? A piece of leather tied to a rusted nail. Like a name. Or a mark. Like a tattoo. And it wasn’t mine. It was the one from the night I came back from the mines, the one I swore I’d never show." His voice cracked. "I didn’t tell nobody. Not even the doctor. Not even the girl I thought I loved."  

The boy stirred the flask with his thumb, eyes sharp as flint. "Then you didn’t just hide it. You wore it. All that time, you kept it under your coat, like it was a promise to yourself — to live, to survive, to remember the night you saw her in the smoke."

Milo didn’t move, didn’t breathe, just stared at the spot where their foreheads had touched, like it was the center of the world. A dry chuckle slipped out of him—low, rough, like a stone scraping across iron. “Seven people,” he said, voice cracking, “and you didn’t tell me until now?”  

“You didn’t ask,” the other muttered, hands pressing into the dirt like he was trying to dig a grave for what they’d been holding in. “I thought you’d be surprised. I thought you’d be mad. Or worse—like I’d betrayed you by wanting this.”  

Then the wind shifted, not with a howl, but with a sudden, sharp gust that made the rusted gate creak and the windmill spin like a drunk man’s arm. One of the women on the porch, her hair pinned back with a silver comb, turned her head and called out, “Milo! The old hayloft’s on fire!” And for a second, the moment didn’t just break—it split, like a bullet through a dry hide. The air went still again, but this time it was full of smoke and the smell of burnt oats, and the two of them stood there, not touching, but already knowing the truth had already passed between them.

Josh slammed the boot down on the dirt, hard enough to make the dust swirl like smoke. The leather cracked, a sound like a gunshot in the quiet. He didn’t look at Joey right away, just stared at the print where the boot had hit—long and ragged, like a hoof had just broken through the ground.  

“Now that’s what I mean,” he said, voice dry as a dried-up creek. “You don’t need to explain it. You just feel it in the bones—like a horse that’s been run too hard, still standing, but not moving. Like you’re waiting for the next kick.”  

Joey didn’t answer. Just pulled his hat low and looked at his boots, then at the sky, where a lone cloud hung like a bruise. The wind picked up, not with a howl, but with a whisper—like someone turning a key in a lock that hadn’t been opened in years.  

And somewhere down the canyon, a bull roared, not at the sun, but at the silence between two men who’d just realized they’d been standing still all along.

The doctor’s hand shook as he lifted the flask, the silver rim catching the lantern light. “I’ll take it easy,” he said, voice rough like old leather, “but I want the whole damn thing done. No half-measures.”  

Josh stood in the doorway, boots scuffed, one arm hooked over the frame, watching the boy’s breath catch in the silence. “You don’t have to be a man to do it,” he said, “just gotta be able to keep still when the world’s on fire.”  

The girl’s fingers fumbled with the edge of her dress, the hem caught on the chair leg. When she finally moved, it wasn’t to pull herself up — it was to reach for the whiskey bottle, to pour a splash into the cracked cup. “I don’t want to be a girl,” she said, “I just want to be sure I don’t disappear.”  

And then she smiled — slow, like a horse breaking from a fence — and it wasn’t pretty. It was the kind of thing that made a man feel like he’d been punched in the ribs and had to keep walking.

The wind snatched the last of the sheriff’s hat and sent it skittering across the dirt like a dead bird. Scott didn’t look. He stepped past the saloon door, boots crunching on gravel, and stopped at the edge of the dry creek bed where the old windmill still stood, rusted and leaning like a drunken man. The tin roof was split down the middle, and the gears creaked when he kicked a stone into the water.

“Still thinkin’ I ain’t got no place in this town?” Scott asked, turning to face the sheriff, who was now wiping his hands on his trousers. The sheriff said nothing, just nodded, then pulled a folded piece of paper from his coat and handed it over. It was a sketch of a woman with a scar across her cheek, and a name scrawled beneath: “Lena Marlowe.”

“You know her?” Scott said, eyes narrowing. “She was in the church when the fire happened. Said she saw a man in the rafters—same one who set the barn on fire.”

The sheriff shrugged. “She ain’t seen no one since. But she’s been lookin’ for you, Scott. Said you were the only one who ever looked at her like she was real.”

The boy shifted in his boots, one hand gripping the worn strap of his saddle bag, the other pressing into the dusty earth like he was trying to sink into it. "Dare so the fuckie had to wait," he muttered, voice dry as a cracked leather belt, "like he wanted something in the sheriff's face." The words didn’t make sense, not really, but they carried weight—like the weight of a dead mule left in the sun. The cowboy didn’t move, just stared at the far end of the canyon where a rusted rail fence sagged like a tired man’s arm.

Then a cough rolled through the dry air, sharp and sudden, like a bullet hitting tin. A red-faced man in a grease-stained hat stumbled from behind a broken barn, boots scuffing the dirt, and the boy saw it then—the red stripe on the man’s sleeve, the one that matched the mark on the sheriff’s old revolver. That was the signal. The boy didn’t speak, just stood and pulled his hat low over his eyes, the dust catching in the brim like ash. The cowboy exhaled slowly, the breath hot and thick, and said, “I didn’t think you’d ever learn to read a sign that wasn’t written in blood.”

The boy turned and looked at the cowboy, eyes narrowed, not with fear but with something sharper—like he’d just seen the ghost of a memory. “You don’t know what it’s like to wait,” he said. “You don’t know what it’s like to feel the wind in your bones and still not know where you’re going.” The cowboy didn’t answer right away. He just sat there, one foot tapping the dirt, waiting for the next word, or the next silence.

The boy kicked the dust off his boots and stepped back, hands on the rusted rail of the old freight car, like he was trying to steady the world. “You mean you didn’t know?” he said, voice low, rough. “I thought you were the one who’d been waiting for that call, the one who’d been watching the track for days.”  

Jamie exhaled, slow and long, and rubbed the back of his neck. “I didn’t know it was you,” he said. “I thought it was just some ghost story from the old ranch, a tale told ‘round the fire when the wind was sharp and the horses wouldn’t stop snorting.”  

Now he looked at the boy, real close, and saw the way the dust caught in his lashes, how his jaw was set like a stubborn gate. “So you’re not just some stranger, then,” Jamie said. “You’re the one who stayed behind when the others packed up and left.”

Darrin straightened up, one hand still gripping Joey’s shoulder, the other brushing the damp edge of his hat. “Now that’s the kind of man you don’t need to explain,” he said, voice low, eyes still locked on Joey’s. “Just show up, do your thing, and the whole damn town knows you’re the one who can’t be pinned down.”  

He stepped back, boots crunching on the dry sand, and pulled a long knife from his belt. The blade caught the light like a shard of broken glass. “I’m goin’ to take the west end of the ranch after dark,” he said, tossing the knife into the water. “Mules are already loose, and the canteen’s dry. If you see a shadow movin’ in the old corral, that’s the one that’s been stealin’ the feed.”  

Joey watched him go, then turned to look at the broken fence post behind them—half-sunk in the mud, half-burnt at the top. A rusted chain dangled from it, still swinging. And there, in the water, where the lapping had made ripples, something glinted: a silver locket, half-submerged, with a name etched in faded script. He didn’t reach for it. Just watched it, waiting to see if it would come back when the wind shifted.

The sheriff’s boots left two smudges on the dirt, one fresh, one already fading like a bad memory. The cowboy stood there, hand still on the saddle horn, watching the dark smear of the night grow longer. His own boots creaked as he stepped back, not because he was cold, but because the wind had shifted and carried the scent of wet horsehide and old meat—like the campfire from two days ago, but sharper, like it was burning inside him.  

He didn’t move to check the saddle, didn’t reach for his flask. Just stood there, breathing in the way he did when he knew something was wrong but didn’t know what. The night wasn’t quiet. It was full of the sound of a distant train, the scrape of a wagon wheel on gravel, and the low hum of a man coughing in a cabin down by the creek.  

Then he saw the light on the porch, a flicker, like a match left too long in the wind. A man in a hat, standing over a rusted oil can, stirring something in a tin pot. The cowboy walked toward it, slow, his boots crunching the dust, and for a second, the man didn’t look up. Then he did—and the cowboy knew, without a word, that the oil wasn’t for the stove. It was for the ground. And the ground was already sputtering.

The boots scraped the dust as he pulled himself up, back to the saddle, one hand still half-dragging on the flank of the old bronco. The horse snorted, a long, lazy sound, like it knew something was off in the air. "You oughta get a real horse," the man muttered, not looking at him, just watching the sun dip behind the ridge like a tired eye. "Not this one. He’s got a mind of his own, and it’s not always on the right side."

He shifted, a grunt slipping past his teeth, and the ache in his lower belly tightened, like a knot in old leather. The wind carried the smell of dry sage and something sour, like old meat left too long in a tin. The sun was already low when the first bullet whistled past, sharp and clean, cutting through the silence like a knife through paper. No one was shouting. Just the rustle of boots on dry ground and the slow, steady beat of a horse's breath.  

The man on the ridge didn't move. Just stared, one hand resting on the hilt of his Colt, the other still half-dangling like he was waiting for something to happen, or for the world to just let go.

The boy groaned low, a sound like gravel shifting under hooves, and shifted just enough to let the cowboy’s hip press deeper into his spine. Sweat slicked the nape of his neck, and the cotton of his shirt stuck to his shoulder like it’d been dipped in oil. The wind didn’t stir much, not with the heat coiling up from the dust and the low, sun-baked earth, but it carried a sharp tang—dirt, wet hay, and something older, like the smell of a dry riverbed after a long drought.

“Yours,” the cowboy growled, voice rough as a worn saddle strap, “wasn’t the first time I saw that kind of hunger in a man’s eyes. But you don’t get it, do you? You think it’s just about the touch—like a man claiming a piece of land. No. It’s about the way a man stands when he’s not afraid to let go. Like you’re not afraid to show your back to the sun.” He pulled back, then pressed in again, slow and sure, and the boy’s breath hitched, his hand gripping the cowboy’s shoulder like he’d never let go.

The sun beat down hard, and the sky hung low, thick as a wet blanket. A lone dust bunny rolled past, caught in the wind, and the boy shifted, his hip pressing against the cowboy’s thigh. They didn’t speak. Just breathed. The world outside—the wind, the distant sound of a mule bridle clink—melted into the silence between them. And the air, thick as tar, still held the heat of what had just happened, and what might still happen.

The trucker exhaled slow and heavy, the sound like a plow dragging through dry dirt, and the air cracked with the snap of a switchblade opening. “You thinkin’ I’m gonna take this slow?” he said, his voice rough, like a saddle worn thin by too many rides. “I’ve been waitin’ for this kind of silence since I left the river town, and I ain’t goin’ back to it now.”

He shifted his weight, one boot dragging on the floorboards, the other still planted like a stake in the ground. The barn’s wood groaned, not from old age, but from the way it had been pressed into shape by a man who knew how to make things stay still—just long enough to let the heat rise, to let the dust settle, to let the world forget it was ever supposed to move.  

The man in the chair didn’t say a word. Just kept his eyes on the crack between the floor and the wall, where a rusted nail had begun to twist, like it was trying to grow roots. And when the trucker finally stepped forward, it wasn’t with a smile. It was with the kind of quiet that comes when you know you’re about to do something that doesn’t belong to either of you.

"Plannin’ together? Yeah, I figured you’d show up with a gun and a story, but not a damn map. I saw the canteen on the porch, half-full, and the name 'Morgan' scribbled on the side. That don’t sound like your hand, boy. You been out there, lookin’ for a ghost or a trail, or just waitin’ for a man to come back from deadwood?"

He stepped into the dust, boots crunchin’ the dry gravel, and the wind snapped the ends of his hat. "You said you knew where the old rusted sign was. I seen it once, back in ’43—bent like a tooth, stuck in the dirt. But it ain’t where you thought. It’s three miles east, past the dry wash where the coyotes howl at night. You don’t go there with a dog, you go there with a dog and a man who don’t believe in ghosts."

He paused, hands shoved in his coat, and looked at the man across from him, eyes hard as old iron. "So you want to go now? Or you want to go with a plan that’s half a dream and half a lie?"

The boy didn’t answer right away. His hands clutched the rough saddle horn, knuckles white, like he was trying to pull himself out of the ground. Scott felt the shift in his chest—tighter, heavier—like a storm had rolled in behind the windbreak. "You’re trembling," he said, voice rougher now, more urgent. "Like you’re about to break."  

The boy exhaled, slow and shaky, and then turned his head just enough to look at Scott, eyes wide and dark in the dusty light. "I’ve been scared," he said, not looking away. "Scared I’d get it wrong. That I’d be too soft, too slow, or just… not enough."  

Scott laughed, a dry, cracked sound, and slapped the boy’s shoulder. "Nothin’ wrong with bein’ soft. You just gotta learn to hold still when it’s all you’ve got." He pulled back slightly, hands still on the boy’s shoulders. "Now come on. Let’s get off this goddamn ridge before the sun sets and the wind starts howling like a damn rattlesnake in a tin can."
