The first man didn’t answer right away, just kept sliding up, slow and sure, like he was measuring the length of the night. The second man grunted again, hand digging into the dirt of the porch floor, his boots scuffing the old wood. A rustle from the barn caught them both—something heavy shifting, a barrel rolling over. Then a sharp cough, like a horse breaking wind, and the wind picked up, carrying the smell of wet hay and rust.  

“Horse’s got a sore leg,” the second man said, eyes still half-lidded, voice rough. “Dropped his foot in the mud last night. Don’t know how he’s still walkin’.”  

The first man pulled back just enough to look at him, then grinned—sharp, unkind, like a man who’d seen too many men break before they ever got to the end of a ride. “Maybe he ain’t walkin’ so much as crawlin’,” he said. “Like us.”  

He pushed back down, hard this time, and the second man gasped, his body jerking like a plow in the mud, the porch creaking beneath them. The wind died. The barn door creaked open and a shadow slipped out—long, lean, with a rifle slung across his back. No word. Just a look. And then silence, thick as dust.

The man shifted his weight, boots scraping the dirt, and spat into the dust. "Flat fury? Yeah, I know what you mean. You ain't talkin' 'bout cattle or a dust storm, you're talkin' about burnin' the whole damn valley clean and settin' it on fire with a single shot." He wiped his jaw with the back of his hand, eyes still fixed on the man behind the fence. "You want the hot cowboys—hot in the saddle, hot in the blood, hot when they ride into a town and don't come out till the wind's changed."

A low chuckle rumbled from the man at the fence, like stones rolling in a dry creek bed. "Then bring 'em. Bring 'em with their boots full of grit and their guns still warm from last night’s fight. Don’t need no fancy talk—just the kind that makes a woman cry and a man run for his life when the sun’s low and the sky’s turnin’ purple."

The wind picked up, snatching at the edges of the old tarp on the trailer, and for a moment, the man’s hat flew off, landing with a thud near a rusted oil can. He didn’t reach for it. Just stood there, watching the dust swirl, like it was the only thing left that hadn’t been broken yet.

Dare took a step back, boots scraping the dry dust, and the horse shivered like it’d just swallowed a bullet. "Apose?" he muttered, blinking at the man, who leaned forward, sweat glistening in the low light. "You mean like the old ways—back when men didn’t talk to horses, just *knew* them?"  

The man nodded, jaw tight, and reached into his coat, pulling out a frayed leather strap with a twisted copper buckle. "I’ve seen it done, once. On a dry creek bed, near the broken saloon. The horse went still, like it was waiting for something to happen. You don’t just *do* it—you *feel* it. Like the wind’s got a name."  

Dare’s hand hovered over the pommel of his saddle, then snapped to his side. "Well, then," he said, voice low, "I guess I’ll try it with the wind in my ears and the sun on my back. If it don’t work, I’ll just go find a new way to fall."

He spat into the dust, wiped his jaw with the back of his hand, and looked down at the canteen in his grip. The leather was dry as a dead man’s tongue, but the water still tasted like it had been stolen from a spring under a storm. “That’s the way I got through the last two summers,” he said, not looking at her, “wore the heat like a second skin. You don’t get used to it—only learned to live with it.”  

She squinted at the horizon where the sun was already dipping behind the mesquite, turning the sky into a smudge of orange and rust. “Then you don at all?” she asked, voice low.  

He pulled his hat low and stepped toward the edge of the dry wash, where the ground cracked like old bone. “Not at all,” he said. “But I know how to move when it’s hot. Know where the wind’s going, where the dust starts to sing. That’s what I’ve got. Not patience. Not peace. Just a kind of stubbornness—like a horse that won’t give up when the trail goes dry.”  

He paused, looked back at her, and grinned again. “Now that I’ve said it, I think I’d rather be hot than cold.”

The boots scraped the dirt like old bones on stone, the heel of his left boot catching on a splintered plank from the old windmill. He didn’t care. The man behind him was still breathing heavy, hands still gripping the leather of the saddle, fingers slick with sweat. One of the boys had pulled a half-empty flask from his coat pocket and was now working the cap between his teeth, the glass trembling as he swayed.  

“Didn’t know you could sweat like that, did you?” the cowboy on the ground muttered, voice rough, like a rope pulled too tight. “I thought you was just some quiet one, like the rest of them.”  

The wind shifted, carrying the smell of hot iron and the faint tang of dried sage from the ridge. A dust devil spiraled past the dry creek bed, and for a second, the two of them were still—just breathing, just heavy, just real. Then the boy on the ground shifted, one knee rolling under the other, and the weight of him pressed harder into the man’s ribs, like a mule trying to get up after a long ride.  

“Gonna take a turn on the next ridge,” the one with the flask said, not looking at the man. “If you don’t want to go, just say so. I don’t mind waiting.”  

No one answered. The boots stayed where they were, heavy, rooted. The sun didn’t rise or set. It just kept burning.

The man in the leather vest shoved the horse's head aside with a grunt, boots scraping the dust like a man trying to bury a bad memory. "You talkin' 'bout real wild, or just the kind that makes a man sweat and forget his name?" he asked, eyes flicking to the rusted gate half-swung open behind them.  

The wind snatched the last of the smoke from the cookout and blew it straight into the eyes of the woman on the porch, who didn't flinch—just pulled a cigarette from her sleeve and lit it with a match that didn’t even need a spark.  

"Hot cowboys," she said, voice flat as a plowshare, "don't need no fancy names. Just need to know what they're for." And then she took a long drag, her fingers pressing into the wood of the porch railing like she was trying to hold on to something that might just disappear.

He pulled the shirt off slow, like it was the last thing he’d ever wear, and the sun caught the edge of his shoulder blade where the old wound still throbbed. The girl on the porch looked up, eyes sharp as a spade, and didn’t flinch when he turned to her, boots caked in dust and blood from last night’s fight. “You ain’t got nothin’ to hide, then,” she said, fingers tapping the rail. “So why’d you come back with that scar on your neck like it was a promise?”

He nodded, looked down at the ground where a dead coyote lay curled in the brush, its ribs showing like a broken signpost. “Because I heard the saloon was still open. And because the woman who ran it used to sing that same song when she poured the whiskey—only this time, it was her own voice that cracked when she said, *I don’t want to be the one who breaks the law.*”  

He turned back, boots scuffing the dirt, and saw the shadow of a man crouched behind the barn, hands gripping a rusted plow. The wind carried a tinny hum—like a radio tuned to nothing—just long enough to make him remember the way the woman used to hum when she wiped the counter. Then he saw her hand on the porch rail, still there, still watching, and he knew he’d come back not to prove anything, but to find out if it was true that love didn’t die when the sun went down.

Dare didn’t move, just kept his eyes on the boy, one hand curled around the worn strap of his rifle, the other resting on the porch rail like he was waiting for something to happen or just hoping the wind would carry the noise away. The boy’s laugh rolled on, deep and unpolished, like a bell rung in a dry canyon. The old man coughed once, wiped his mouth on his shirt, and muttered, “Well, I’ll be damned. That’s the kind of thing you don’t see in a town that hasn’t seen a real war.”  

The boy’s dad stepped forward, boots scuffing the dirt, and said, “You think I didn’t see it too? I saw it the first time he pulled that damn lasso from the ground and didn’t know which end was tight.” He looked at the boy, real close now, like he was trying to read the crack in his eyes. “You don’t have to explain it, kid. Just keep it going. That’s what he wanted—more of it, not a clean end.”  

Then the boy turned and walked into the shadow of the barn, his boots clattering like a dead horse’s hooves on stone, and Dare heard the rustle of something long and dry—like a horse’s tail dragged through dust—before the silence fell like a blanket, thick and full of unspoken things.

The sweat on Josh’s back stung like a slap, and he groaned, shifting his hips just enough to catch the boy’s knee in the motion. The saddle leather scraped against the edge of the wagon, a sharp crack echoing through the dust-choked air. “You’re gonna make the whole herd jump,” he muttered, voice thick with both exhaustion and the raw heat of the moment.

The boy didn’t answer—just pulled his legs tighter around Josh’s waist, one hand braced on the old horse’s neck, the other digging into the soft patch of hair at the base of his spine. A flicker of something sharp passed between them, like a bullet missed its mark but still left a bruise. The wind came in hot and dry, carrying the smell of dry grass and something sour—maybe old whiskey, maybe just the dirt in the hollow.

Josh exhaled, slow and heavy, and when he moved again, it wasn’ smooth. The motion was clumsy, like a man trying to ride a mule that hadn’t been broken in years. But it worked—just enough to make the boy gasp, to make the world tilt, and for a second, the stars above didn’t look like stars at all, just hot dots burning in a black canvas.

Jonah slammed the front door shut, the wood groaning like a man in pain, and the boy sat on the porch step, knees drawn up, one hand clutching a rusted horseshoe he’d been chewing on. The wind picked up, snatching at the ragged edge of his shirt, and the boy didn’t move. 

“Still got that thing in your pocket?” Jonah asked, leaning against the rail, boots scuffing the dust. “The one that smells like old grease and fear?”  

The boy nodded slowly, eyes fixed on the cracked porch board where a bird had been trying to peck through the splintered wood for hours. “Yeah,” he said. “And I ain’t got no other.”
